note: Faithful rendering of the Madhyamaka argument that past, future and present mind cannot be the object of self-grasping, with the plantain and barren woman's son examples correctly handled.

errors.english: For the act of requesting and dual actions
errors.why: This is the jñaptidvitīya karman, an act with a motion and one proclamation, not 'requesting and dual actions'.

fix.find: For the act of requesting and dual actions
fix.replace: For an act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (jñaptidvitīya karman)

errors.english: For the act of requesting and fourfold actions
errors.why: This is the jñapticaturtha karman, an act with a motion and three proclamations (four in all), not 'requesting and fourfold actions'.

fix.find: For the act of requesting and fourfold actions
fix.replace: For an act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (jñapticaturtha karman)

note: The Upāli boundary passage is followed correctly, but the standard Vinaya names of the saṅghakarman types are garbled and several of the grammatical glosses are left obscure.

errors.english: It is the very engagement of the mind with an entity that, by producing an incompatible cause in the nature of a latent tendency (vasana) habitual imprint or predisposition, causes the mind that perceives the absence of an entity to cut the continuity.
errors.why: It is the cognition of non-entity that, by producing an incompatible cause (a vāsanā), cuts off the continuum of the cognition of the entity; the English reverses which cognition produces and which is cut.

errors.english: just as coldness comes from fire at that time
errors.why: The simile is cold being removed by fire (fire opposing cold), not cold arising from fire.

note: The argument about the contradiction of non-coexistence between conceptions is roughly followed, but the direction of the opposition is muddled in key places and unmarked inline glosses clutter the text.

errors.english: How can the effect be hollow just because the cause is hollow?
errors.why: The question is how the cause (pradhāna) is hollow because the effect is hollow; the English reverses the direction of the inference.

fix.find: How can the effect be hollow just because the cause is hollow?
fix.replace: How is it that, because the effect is hollow, that [cause] too is hollow?

errors.english: whatever falls within the path of vision—such as pleasure groves or parks—is the (pradhana) primary matrix/nature and is also utterly hollow
errors.why: The quoted Sāṃkhya verse says that what comes into view is utterly hollow (and hence, the commentary argues, the pradhāna too); it does not identify what is seen with the pradhāna.

note: The Sāṃkhya refutation is mostly followed, but one reversal of the argument's direction and a misparse of the quoted verse need correction.

errors.english: For the sake of illustration, to benefit the world
errors.why: The line says the Buddha spoke 'illuminating the excellence of [giving]'; that is lost and replaced by 'to benefit the world'.

errors.english: the Jewel among Men born for the sake of the world's happiness
errors.why: bde bar 'gro ba renders sugata (Skt. prakaṭitasugataḥ): a jewel of a man who manifests as a Sugata is born, not one born 'for the world's happiness'.

note: The colophon and the opening verses on Sāketa are serviceable, but the Sugata reference and the 'excellence of giving' line are lost, and a stray editorial phrase ends the text.

errors.english: that son of an ascetic also caused the Blessed One, who had attained awakening, to realize his hoped-for aspiration for the fruit of Worthy One (Arhat)
errors.why: The Blessed One (ergative) caused the ascetic's son to attain the arhatship he hoped for, not the reverse.

fix.find: that son of an ascetic also caused the Blessed One, who had attained awakening, to realize his hoped-for aspiration for the fruit of Worthy One (Arhat)
fix.replace: the Blessed One, having attained awakening, caused that son of an ascetic to attain the fruit of a Worthy One (Arhat) that he had hoped for

errors.english: For those of great wisdom and steady, grave minds, beings like you are not easily found.
errors.why: The qualities describe the addressees: the appearance of such steadfast, grave-minded, greatly wise ones as you is hard to find.

errors.english: the Guru of the Gods, the Lord of the Immortals [note: Indra]
errors.why: The comparison is to the guru of the gods (Bṛhaspati), preceptor of the lord of the immortals; the note wrongly makes the guru Indra.

note: The verses and the new jātaka opening are mostly right, but the closing prose inverts who brought whom to arhatship.
Sound rendering of the argument against the variegated whole and successive-perception superimposition; the root verses are kept distinct, though a stray inline gloss on avayavin needs cleaning.

errors.english: such as those that are mistaken [note: original: "'khrul pa", (bhrānta)]
errors.why: In the theory of pseudo-reasons 'khrul pa is vyabhicāra, deviation (inconclusiveness), not bhrānta 'mistaken'.

fix.find: such as those that are mistaken [note: original: "'khrul pa", (bhrānta)]
fix.replace: of those that are deviant (inconclusive) and so forth [note: original: "'khrul pa", (vyabhicāra)]

errors.english: Since merely enumerating all the members
errors.why: rnam grangs here is paryāya: all the members would be, as a mere synonym, 'provers of the probandum'; it is not about enumerating them.

note: A careful rendering of the dispute over qualifying the statement of similarity, with the general rule and exception argument correctly structured; the logical term for deviance needs fixing.

errors.why: gzhal bya is prameya, the object of valid cognition, not jñeya (shes bya).

note: The apoha discussion and the siddhasādhana point about isolated words are well rendered; one wrong Sanskrit equivalent and a stray editorial phrase at the end.

errors.english: Destruction is not brought about by another agent but occurs due to the inherent nature of things.
errors.why: gzhan rtsom pa means originating another [whole]: without originating another, the thing itself perishes by its nature; it is not about another agent of destruction.

errors.english: because one does not see destruction in wood merely from contact with fire
errors.why: What is not seen in wood destroyed by contact with fire is division into parts; the wood's destruction itself is not denied.

errors.english: that which has parts is not without cause
errors.why: Because there is no cause (or proof), there is no whole (avayavin); the English inverts this into 'the whole is not without cause'.

note: The anti-atomist argument is broadly followed, but several clauses about destruction and the whole are misparsed in ways that change the argument.
